heading: An unbroken line of temple builders
body: Tamil Nadu's distinguishing feature is continuity: a Dravidian temple-building tradition that runs, without a real break, from rock-cut caves in the 7th century to the towering gopurams still being expanded today. It starts with the Pallava dynasty, which ruled from the 3rd to 9th centuries CE and pioneered the shift from carving temples directly out of rock to building free-standing structural ones — the Shore Temple and the monolithic Pancha Rathas at Mahabalipuram, and the Kailasanatha temple at their capital Kanchipuram, are the clearest surviving evidence of that transition, and they set the architectural vocabulary — the vimana tower, the pillared mandapa hall, the gateway gopuram — that every later Tamil dynasty would keep building in.

The Cholas took that vocabulary to an imperial scale. From roughly the 9th to 13th centuries they built a maritime empire that ran naval trade routes as far as Southeast Asia and China, and at its most aggressive, in 1025 CE, Rajendra Chola I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal to attack the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra and Malaysia — a strike historians still debate the motive for, whether protecting Tamil merchant guilds' access to the China trade or asserting naval prestige, but which remains the only large-scale long-distance naval campaign launched from South Asia in the historical record. On land, the same dynasty built the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur in 1010 CE under Rajaraja I, a 216-foot granite tower that, together with two related 11th- and 12th-century Chola temples at Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram, forms the UNESCO World Heritage site known as the Great Living Chola Temples.

The Pandyas, ruling contemporaneously and later from Madurai, contributed their own body of rock-cut and structural temples before falling to repeated wars with the Chalukyas and finally the Cholas. What makes Tamil Nadu unusual on the subcontinent is that this temple-building habit never really stopped after the classical dynasties fell — later Vijayanagara-era and Nayak-era rulers kept adding gopurams and halls to Pallava- and Chola-founded temple complexes for centuries, so a single site can carry visibly different eras of construction stacked on top of one another.

The entries on the map trace that same line forward: Pallava cave and rock-cut temples, Chola imperial temple architecture, and the later additions that kept the tradition alive well past any one dynasty's collapse.
